sb_prompt: WHAT DO YOU THINK ABOUT CURRENT OR RECENT AMERICAN ACTIONS IN LATIN AMERICA
turns: Yeah, how's that call to Mexico went for you? I got a tip to call a cousin there, thought it'd be cool to hear about the place.

It wasn't Mexico, it was Guatemala, but yeah, same deal. I grew up in a little town there, you know? My dad was a plumber over there too, so I helped him fix pipes in the old house before I knew I wanted to be a plumber myself. It was just... normal. Like breathing. I never really thought about it until later, but now it hits me sometimes.

Oh wow, really? That's actually really cool, I never thought about how much I took it for granted until I left. My mom is a waitress here, so I worked summers at ten years old just to save up for gas, and honestly, the tips can be brutal sometimes, but hearing that you did the same job as your dad there... that's a whole different story, right?

Yeah, it's like... my dad didn't even think it was a "career" back then, he just said "fix what's broken," and here I am trying to fix these big city pipes while remembering fixing a sink in a bathroom with dirt floors. It's weird, right? You think you chose a path, but sometimes it's just what's right in front of you when you grow up.

Yeah, that's the thing, it's not like I chose to serve people, I just picked up the first job that paid enough to eat, but honestly, watching my mom get yelled at by a regular because a table wasn't cleaned fast enough... it makes me wonder if that's just how everyone is there, or if it's just how we are here. Do people in your town get mad at plumbers too, or is it more like they just appreciate you fixing things?

Yeah, usually nobody gets mad, they just come out of their houses or offices when the sink stops working or the water won't flush, it's like, "Hey, can you fix this?" not "why is this broken?" but sometimes if the pressure is too low or the bill is too high... yeah, people get real loud about it.
Yeah, here it's more like "why isn't this table clean yet?" and then you just have to smile and take the heat, even if you cleaned it twice.
Yeah, it's just that kind of expectation, you know? Like, if the water doesn't show up, you feel it right away, but if a table isn't clean, well, people forget to eat sometimes anyway.

Yeah, I totally get that, like you can't really hold a table hostage if they haven't tipped yet, but I feel like people here just assume you owe them patience for free, whereas in Guatemala it sounds like you're actually solving a problem that matters to them right then and there.

Yeah, it's just that immediate, like if the water stops you feel it in your stomach, but here it's more like "wait, can we just talk about the menu for five minutes" which is harder for me because my legs are shaking from standing all day.

Yeah, I get that, but honestly, when I see a customer drop a $50 tip for a whole meal, it feels like they're paying for the whole experience, not just the food, so maybe the pressure is different there?
Yeah, exactly, it's like the water is just part of the house, you know, if it stops it's an emergency, but here people just keep eating and complaining about the price while ignoring the mess.

Yeah, but I mean, the $50 tip is just... it doesn't come with a receipt or anything, so you kinda feel like you gotta prove you deserved it before they walk out, whereas fixing a leak is instant relief, so the gratitude feels more real there.
Yeah, but I guess I just don't get the feeling that they expect me to carry the whole weight of their stress, like you guys seem to do with the tables.
Yeah, but I guess it's just that in here, nobody tells you to take a break, they just keep yelling at you while you stand there sweating.

Yeah, but I guess sometimes I still wish there was more of that "thank you" out here, like maybe if I told a customer how hard the line was during the storm they'd be more patient, but I just keep fixing the valve and hoping they leave the bill alone.
Yeah, but I guess if you don't feel the weight of it, you don't really see how heavy it is, so maybe that's why you don't complain as much.

Yeah, but maybe the reason I don't complain is because fixing the pipe is so final, like the water either works or it doesn't, there's no guessing game, whereas serving people feels like you're just guessing what they want forever.
Yeah, but maybe that's why you don't stress about the customers, since the pipe either works or it doesn't, but here it feels like you're never done.

Yeah, but maybe I just don't get tired of being right, you know? Like if I'm done, the water's done, so I can go home and actually sit down, whereas out here, even if you leave the table, they might just call you back in ten minutes because they still feel something's wrong.
Yeah, I guess being "done" feels real good sometimes, especially when you don't have to worry about getting yelled at for being slow.
Yeah, but I guess sometimes when the water finally turns back on, the whole day just feels over, you know? Like a hard line in the sand.
Yeah, I guess once the table finally clears, you can actually sit down for a second, and that feels kinda rare too.
Yeah, it's just that once the water runs clear, there's nothing left to do but maybe go home and watch TV, but out here you're just waiting for the next table and it never really ends.
Yeah, but maybe the real difference is that once the water runs, you're actually free, whereas out here I still have to worry about the check and if they're going to leave a tip or walk out on me.
Yeah, that's the scary part, isn't it? You fix it once, and you're free, but out here, you never know if they're just done or if they're just waiting to see if you can fix it again for free.
That is exactly the thing that keeps me up, you never know if you actually made it worth their while.
Yeah, but honestly, I just fix the pipe and then I go home, I don't have to chase them down or see their face tomorrow.
Yeah, but I guess the part that bugs me is that you can't just turn off a customer if you didn't like the shift, you gotta wait till the end of the day and hope they don't come back tomorrow.
Yeah, but you at least get a moment where you're not just waiting for the next problem, you actually win, don't you?
Yeah, but I guess the scary part is that if they leave a bad tip, you can't just say "the table wasn't clean" and walk away, you have to keep smiling while they argue about it.
Yeah, but I guess the real difference is that I can just leave the job done, so I don't have to look anyone in the eye after I hang up the wrench.
Yeah, but I guess the real difference is that once the water runs, you're actually free, whereas out here I still have to worry about the check and if they're going to leave a tip or walk out on me.
Yeah, but you know what? Maybe it's just that the water doesn't care if you're tired or not, it either flows or it doesn't, so I don't have to worry about making them happy anymore.
Yeah, but that sounds kinda nice too, being able to just... stop and leave it there.
Yeah, I mean, once the water flows, you don't have to wonder if they'll come back angry, so it's just... done, right?
Yeah, but I guess that's the thing where my legs hurt so much I don't even care anymore, if you don't have to explain it to someone's face, maybe it's better to just leave it there.
Yeah, but maybe that's exactly why I chose it, because once the water flows, you don't have to wonder if they'll come back angry, so it's just... done, right?
Yeah, maybe that's the only reason it feels good to me, knowing you can just turn the wrench off and walk away without looking at anyone.
Yeah, maybe that's why I don't feel like I'm carrying the world on my shoulders anymore.
